topic: Geometric Interpretation of Non-Square Matrices: Dimensional Portals
target_audience: University students (Linear Algebra) or advanced High School students

sections.title: The Dimensional Portal Concept
sections.content: Introduce the idea that while square matrices transform space within the same dimension (like rotating or stretching a 2D sheet), non-square matrices act as 'portals' that transport vectors between different dimensional worlds. Establish the character 'Pixel the Cat' who lives in a 2D grid.
sections.example: Pixel the Cat is a flat 2D drawing. We want to see what happens when he moves into a 3D world or gets compressed into a 1D line.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Basis Vectors as a Map
sections.content: Briefly review that the columns of any matrix tell us where the unit basis vectors (i-hat and j-hat) land after the transformation. This is the 'DNA' of the transformation.
sections.example: In a 2D square matrix, i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1) land somewhere else on the 2D plane. Animation: Show the grid lines following these landing spots.

sections.title: Tall Matrices: Upgrading Dimensions (2D to 3D)
sections.content: Explain the 3x2 matrix. The input has 2 coordinates (2D), but the output has 3 coordinates (3D). Geometrically, this means we are taking a 2D plane and embedding it into a 3D space. Key insight: The transformation maps the 2D world onto a slanted 'sheet' inside the 3D volume.
sections.example: Matrix A = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]. Pixel the Cat is mapped into 3D space. His original flat body now exists on a tilted plane where his height (z) depends on his x and y coordinates.

sections.title: Wide Matrices: Downgrading Dimensions (3D to 2D)
sections.content: Explain the 2x3 matrix. The input is a 3D vector, but the output only has 2 coordinates. Geometrically, this represents a projection or a 'squishing' of 3D space onto a 2D plane. Information is lost (the kernel/null space).
sections.example: A 3D bird flying in the sky. A 2x3 matrix acts like a flashlight from above, casting the bird's shadow onto the flat ground. The shadow is a 2D representation of the 3D bird.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Row x Column Logic
sections.content: Connect the visual to the math. In an M x N matrix, N is the dimension of the 'input' space (starting world) and M is the dimension of the 'output' space (destination world). Show how the number of columns dictates how many 'starting' directions we have.
sections.example: A 1x3 matrix: Input is 3D space, output is a 1D number line. Visual: An entire 3D room being sucked into a single infinite string.

sections.title: Summary: The Column Space Perspective
sections.content: Wrap up by reinforcing that the columns of a non-square matrix span a subspace in the destination dimension. The transformation is just a movement from one coordinate system to another.
sections.example: Animation: A split-screen showing Pixel the Cat jumping through a 3x2 matrix 'portal' into a 3D room, and a 3D Bird being projected through a 2x3 matrix 'portal' onto Pixel's 2D floor.
